resume: Built an in-browser quantum computing lab for problem statement SIH26140 with Team X FORCE: a 12-qubit statevector simulator with two-way circuit ↔ code sync for OpenQASM 3, Qiskit, Cirq and PennyLane.
Verified against Qiskit Aer on 22 circuits (max deviation 6.66 × 10^−16); 448 Vitest tests assert every physics claim in the lessons.
Self-checking AI tutor runs its answers on the simulator and drops any that disagree; 1,090 offline topics; ships as an Android APK.

readme.heading: Overview
readme.text: Qurious Learn quantum computing by building it. Smart India Hackathon 2026 SIH26140 Team X FORCE AI-Based Interactive Quantum Algorithm Learning Platform Smart Education. A quantum lab, a self-checking AI tutor and a real-machine noise simulator in one app. It runs in a browser and installs as an offline Android APK.

readme.heading: What it does
readme.text: Build circuits and watch the state. Drag or tap gates onto a canvas. A full statevector simulator runs on the device — up to 12 qubits, no server, no account. Amplitudes, Bloch spheres, measurement outcomes and a probability table update as you go. Write it as code, either way round. The same circuit exports to OpenQASM 3, Qiskit, Cirq and PennyLane. Edit the code and the canvas rebuilds; edit the canvas and the code follows. Both write the same object, so they cannot drift apart. A tutor that checks itself. It proposes an answer, runs it on the simulator, and throws the answer away if the output disagrees with the claim. With no network it answers from 1,090 topics: 193 written by hand, and 897 that it computes on the spot by running the circuit in question, so they cannot contradict the simulator. It labels which of the three — written, computed, or a configured language model — produced the answer. The Noise Lab. Run your circuit the way a real machine would — depolarising Pauli errors, amplitude damping, dephasing and readout flips, as Monte Carlo trajectories. A Bell state at today's superconducting error rates produces |01⟩ and |10⟩, outcomes ideal physics forbids. Four presets: Ideal, Trapped ion, Today's superconducting, Early hardware. Graded on physics, not on string matching. Challenges compare the state your circuit produces against the target with a global-phase-in

readme.heading: Correctness
readme.text: The simulator is cross-checked against Qiskit Aer over 22 circuits. Worst disagreement: 6.66 × 10⁻¹⁶. Lesson content is held to the same standard: tests/algorithms.test.ts asserts every physics claim the algorithm lessons make against the simulator, so prose that lies about its own circuit fails the build. Phase estimation gets a second, independent check — its bit ordering is confirmed against Qiskit rather than against our own engine, because a shared misunderstanding between simulator and test would otherwise go unnoticed.

readme.text: DeepGuard looks at the faces in a photo or a video and tells you whether they show signs of being AI-generated. It does not just give a verdict: it shows the evidence (where in the face the signal sits, how the check was made) and explains it in plain language. The answer is a statistical signal, not proof. One Python engine and one API serve every client: the website, a Windows desktop app, an Android app, an iPhone home-screen app, a Telegram bot, and signed PDF reports that anyone can verify.

Voice never auto-saves: every spoken command is parsed and shown in a confirmation. dialog (with editable quantity / product / tier) before anything changes. readme.heading: Thozhan
readme.text: A self-hosted voice assistant that speaks Tanglish — Tamil-English code-mixed speech — and drives a lip-synced 3D avatar. Everything runs on your own machine. No cloud APIs, no telemetry, no account. Status: scaffold. The model calls are stubbed and nothing speaks yet. The architecture, algorithms and instrumentation are written and tested; the four model backends are not. See Current status before you invest time in this.

readme.heading: What it is
readme.text: Six stages in a loop: Capture microphone audio, segmented into utterances by a voice activity. detector and a semantic endpointer. Transcribe with Whisper.cpp, streaming, while the user is still talking. Generate a reply with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct via llama.cpp. Synthesise speech with XTTS-v2, using a cloned voice. Extract visemes — mouth shapes — from the synthesised audio. Stream those to a browser page that applies them as morph-target weights on a. GLB avatar. The stages are streamed and overlapped: the LLM's first clause goes to TTS while it is still writing the second, so the avatar starts speaking before the reply is finished.

readme.heading: Why Tanglish
readme.text: Bilingual Tamil speakers do not speak Tamil or English. They speak both in the same sentence — "naan meeting ku poren", "call panniten", "adhu configure panna mudiyala". Assistants force a choice: pick a language, get a monolingual response. Answering in either pure Tamil or pure English sounds equally unnatural to someone who talks like that. This turns out to be hard, and the difficulty is not evenly spread: Whisper has no code-mixed training data. It returns the same utterance as. Tamil script one time and romanised the next, and occasionally translates. Llama 3.1 has some Tamil in its pretraining mix, but not much. It drifts. back to English after a few turns. XTTS-v2 takes one language code per call and applies one phonemiser to the. whole string. There is no Tanglish setting. Three answers are implemented, and one is not: thozhan/phonemes.py removes the XTTS problem by. phonemising Tamil and English separately into one shared IPA inventory, so there is no language left to declare. Includes Tamil's positional voicing — the plosive series க ச ட த ப has four surface realisations depending on context, and getting that wrong is most of what makes Indian TTS sound flat. thozhan/codemix.py makes mixing measurable and. controllable: per-token language identification for romanised Tamil, the Gambäck & Das Code-Mixing Index, and a controller that steers generation towards a target

readme.heading: Why offline
readme.text: Latency. A round trip to a cloud API is 200-800 ms before the model does. any work. In a voice loop with four model calls, that is the difference between a conversation and a walkie-talkie. Privacy. Everything a voice assistant hears is by definition ambient audio. from your home. That should not leave the machine. Cost. Four models per turn against metered APIs adds up fast, and the. usage pattern — bursty, conversational — is the worst case for per-token billing. It keeps working. No API deprecations, no rate limits, no service going. away. The cost is that you need a GPU and about 8 GB of disk for weights.

readme.heading: Latency is the metric
readme.text: A voice assistant that answers correctly in four seconds feels broken. The number that matters is time to first audio: the gap between you finishing your sentence and the avatar starting to speak. Everything after that overlaps with playback. pipeline.py records per-stage timings for every turn and writes them to logs/latency.jsonl. Stage: Naive, With what is implemented. End-of-turn detection: ~700 ms fixed VAD tail, ~150-300 ms, semantic. Whisper large-v3, 3 s utterance: ~300 ms, ~50 ms, streamed during speech. Llama time-to-first-token: ~150 ms, ~150 ms. First speakable chunk generated: ~400 ms sentence, ~200 ms clause. XTTS-v2 first audio chunk: ~400 ms, ~400 ms. Visemes for first chunk: ~50 ms, ~50 ms. Time to first audio: ~2000 ms, ~1000 ms. None of these have been measured. The left column is taken from published benchmarks of the individual components; the right column is what the architecture should manage once the model backends exist. Finding out how wrong both are is what bench/harness.py is for — it enforces declared budgets and exits non-zero when one is exceeded.

readme.heading: Current status
readme.text: Scaffold. Structure, algorithms, orchestration and instrumentation are written and tested. Every model call is stubbed.

readme.heading: Implemented and tested
readme.text: Component: File. Config, .env loading, cross-field validation: config.py. Pipeline orchestration, async wiring, barge-in task cancellation: pipeline.py. Latency instrumentation and percentiles: pipeline.py. LocalAgreement-2 streaming policy and buffer management: streaming.py. Semantic endpointing, Tanglish-aware: turndetect.py. Sentence and clause chunking: llm.py. Language tagging, CMI, switch-point fraction, bias controller: codemix.py. Tamil G2P with positional voicing; unified Tamil+English inventory: phonemes.py. WER, CER, script-blind phoneme error rate, latency, lip-sync metrics: metrics.py. ARKit blendshapes, dominance coarticulation, mel features: blendshapes.py. Episodic and semantic memory, hashing embedder, vector search: memory.py. Tool registry, schema generation, risk gating: tools.py. VRAM budgeting, residency planning, GPU probing: residency.py. Barge-in detection and conversation state machine: aec.py. Viseme data model and wire format: visemes.py. Corpus manifest, validation, speaker-disjoint splits: bench/datasets.py. Benchmark harness with budgets and baseline comparison: bench/harness.py. Browser avatar: morph targets, audio clock, procedural life: web/main.js.

readme.heading: Stubbed
readme.text: Component: File. Microphone capture and VAD: stt.py. Whisper.cpp transcription: stt.py, streaming.py. llama.cpp generation, speculative prefill: llm.py. XTTS-v2 synthesis and playback: tts.py. Viseme extraction, both backends: visemes.py. Websocket server: visemes.py. Neural blendshape inference: blendshapes.py. Echo cancellation: aec.py. Fact extraction, tool implementations: memory.py, tools.py. CUDA auto-detection: config.py.

readme.heading: Does not exist
readme.text: The Tanglish speech corpus. Tooling is written; the recordings are not. Every trained checkpoint — the Whisper LoRA, the LLM LoRA, the turn. detector, the blendshape model. Training scripts are in scripts/; none has been run. Stubs raise NotImplementedError rather than returning plausible-looking values. Running python -m thozhan.pipeline today gets as far as building the stage objects and then stops on the first stub it hits. That is the intended behaviour for a scaffold: a stage that fakes its output makes the whole system look like it works. Every stub carries TODO comments describing the intended approach, including the parts that are still open questions.

readme.text: Python 3.11+. An NVIDIA GPU with 12 GB VRAM, or patience. ~8 GB disk for model weights. A working microphone and speakers.

readme.heading: Check the VRAM budget first

readme.heading: Models
readme.text: The script downloads nothing by default — every command in it is commented out. Read it, uncomment what you want, and run it. It covers Whisper ggml weights, the Llama 3.1 8B GGUF, and the XTTS-v2 checkpoint, with notes on quantisation choices and licences. Two licences to be aware of before you build on this: Llama 3.1 is under the Meta Llama 3.1 Community License, not a standard. open-source licence. XTTS-v2 is under the Coqui Public Model License, which restricts. commercial use.

readme.heading: Tests
readme.text: 477 tests, covering everything implemented. The pipeline tests run the full orchestration against fake stages, so they pass on a machine with no GPU and no weights. Stubs are asserted to raise rather than to return anything.

readme.heading: Hardware
readme.text: Development target — Lenovo LOQ, RTX 4070 Laptop (8 GB VRAM), 16 GB RAM. VRAM is the binding constraint. thozhan/residency.py does this arithmetic properly, including activation memory, which back-of-envelope budgets routinely forget: Llama 3.1 8B Q4KM @ 8k ctx, with KV cache: ~5.9 GB. Whisper large-v3, with activations: ~2.5 GB. XTTS-v2, with activations: ~2.2 GB. Total: ~10.6 GB. That does not fit in 8 GB, and it does not fit after moving Whisper to the CPU either. The planner will tell you a plan "fits" while having pushed the LLM off the GPU — check plan.viable, not plan.fits, because a 15× slower LLM is not an assistant. suggestalternatives() lists the real options: smaller Whisper, lower LLAMANCTX, or a harsher quant, with the quality cost of each noted. Some 4070 Laptop configurations ship 12 GB, in which case everything fits. Stretch goal — run a quantised build on cheap hardware. Not attempted. See ROADMAP.md phase 8.

readme.heading: Roadmap
readme.text: See ROADMAP.md for the full sequencing, with the prerequisites and open questions for each phase. The short version: One turn, end to end. Nothing else matters until this works. The avatar moves — websocket server plus the crude viseme path. Latency — semantic endpointing, streaming STT, clause chunking. All three. implemented, none measured. The corpus. The highest-value missing piece, and the one thing that. cannot be shortcut with more code. Tanglish quality — the fine-tunes and the controllable mixing ratio. Blocked. on 3. Real lip sync. Data problem is easy here; worth doing early. Barge-in. Blocked on echo cancellation. Memory and tools. Cheap hardware.
